entities.name: Medius of Larissa
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Medius of Larissa, son of Oxythemis, a Thessalian nobleman, emerged as a pivotal naval and military commander in the tumultuous Hellenistic period, specifically during the Wars of the Diadochi. His career, spanning the late 4th and early 3rd centuries BCE, saw him serve as a trusted companion of Alexander the Great and later as a key admiral and advisor to Antigonus I Monophthalmus, whose ambitions profoundly shaped the post-Alexandrian world. Medius's strategic acumen in naval warfare and his political influence at the courts of these powerful rulers underscore his significance in the fragmentation and re-formation of Alexander's vast empire.

Medius initially served Alexander, notably participating in the Indian campaigns and potentially in the naval preparations for the circumnavigation of Arabia. After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, he quickly aligned himself with Antigonus Monophthalmus, becoming one of his most reliable commanders. His most celebrated achievement was the decisive naval victory at the Battle of Salamis in Cyprus in 306 BCE, where he commanded Antigonus's fleet against Ptolemy I Soter's forces. This victory, involving over 150 warships on each side, led to Antigonus and his son Demetrius Poliorcetes assuming royal titles, a critical step in the formal dissolution of Alexander's unified empire and the establishment of independent Hellenistic kingdoms. He also played a significant role in the protracted Siege of Rhodes (305-304 BCE).
